title: Medicaid Eligibility in 2027: Revenue Cycle Needs to Prepare for More Eligibility Risk
summary: Medicaid eligibility in 2027 will require more active Revenue Cycle monitoring. Long-stay patients need repeat verification, work-queue triggers, proactive redetermination tracking, and clear ownership.
body_markdown:
Medicaid eligibility has never been static.


Coverage can become active, lapse, renew, or change while a patient is still receiving care. Beginning in 2027, that variability becomes even more important for Revenue Cycle leaders to watch.


CMS is implementing major Medicaid eligibility changes beginning January 1, 2027. Certain adults will be subject to new community-engagement requirements, and adults in the Medicaid expansion group will move to six-month eligibility redeterminations.


For hospitals, the operational question is simple:


**Are we treating Medicaid eligibility as a one-time registration check, or as an ongoing Revenue Cycle control?**


From my experience, the biggest breakdowns happen at two points.


The first is before coverage is established.


The second is after everyone assumes coverage is settled.


## Start With the Most Basic Question: Is the Patient Eligible?


When a patient presents without active Medicaid coverage, the first question should be:


**Is this patient potentially Medicaid eligible?**


If the answer may be yes, there needs to be a clear process for determining eligibility and beginning the appropriate application, enrollment, or financial-clearance process.


Who identifies the potential eligibility?


Who starts the process?


Who follows up for missing information?


Who communicates with the patient or family?


And who continues working the account while eligibility remains unresolved?


Those responsibilities should be clear before the account becomes a billing problem.


The 2027 changes add another layer because certain adults will need to meet new Medicaid community-engagement requirements, while CMS also identifies numerous exemptions and exceptions.


That means hospitals should be careful not to assume why coverage appears inactive.


**Verify first.**


## Eligibility Should Not Be a One-Time Admission Check


One of the biggest process failures I have seen occurs during long inpatient stays.


Eligibility is verified at admission.


The account is considered covered.


And then no one checks it again.


That is where risk builds.


Coverage can change during a prolonged hospitalization. A renewal can come due. Information may be requested. Eligibility can lapse.


If the organization discovers the problem only after discharge—or when Billing is ready to submit the claim—it may already have lost the best opportunity to resolve the issue while the patient and family are accessible.


For long-stay patients, I recommend **rechecking Medicaid eligibility at least every 30 days** .


That is an operational recommendation, not a CMS requirement.


The workflow should be simple:


**Eligibility verified at admission → Recheck at least every 30 days → Any change, update, or lapse triggers a work queue → Eligibility team acts**


The goal is not another report.


The goal is to create work automatically when something changes.


## Capture the Redetermination Date Before It Becomes a Problem


Beginning in 2027, Medicaid adult expansion beneficiaries subject to the new requirement will generally move to six-month eligibility periods and redeterminations. CMS guidance also notes that states may start renewal activity well before the end of the eligibility period.


If a patient’s next redetermination date is available, Revenue Cycle should capture it.


Do not wait for eligibility to come back inactive.


If capacity allows, I would begin proactive review **30 days before the expected redetermination date** .


If that is not operationally feasible, I would make **15 days before** the minimum target.


Those are Revenue Cycle controls, not federal deadlines.


The point is to give the team time to identify a problem before coverage actually lapses.


## A Change in Coverage Should Create Immediate Work


Once an eligibility change is identified for a patient who is still in-house, I would expect the centralized eligibility or financial-clearance team to begin follow-up **by the next business day** .


That is when the organization has the best opportunity to resolve the issue.


The patient may still be available.


Family members or authorized representatives may still be reachable.


The care team may be able to help connect the appropriate people.


And there is still time to address the issue before the account reaches Billing.


If coverage has lapsed, the team responsible for eligibility should continue to own the resolution.


It should not automatically become a back-end problem simply because coverage changed.


## Three Attempts Should Lead to Escalation, Not a Parking Place


If additional information is required and the patient or family cannot initially be reached, I recommend **up to three documented outreach attempts** .


If those attempts are unsuccessful, the account should move to:


**Eligibility Unresolved**


But that status should trigger escalation.


It should not simply become another place for the account to sit.


The escalation path should be designed to make actual contact with a family member, authorized representative, or other designee who can help coordinate financial clearance.


The purpose is resolution—not simply documenting that the patient did not respond.


## Ownership Should Stay With the Team Best Positioned to Resolve the Issue


If the patient is still in-house, the centralized eligibility or financial-clearance team should own the coverage issue.


If eligibility has lapsed, the team responsible for eligibility should continue working toward resolution.


If the patient has discharged and the account remains unbilled, Billing may be the first team to identify that there is still a coverage problem.


But that does not mean Billing becomes the new owner of Medicaid eligibility.


Billing should partner with the front-end eligibility team to determine how the issue can be resolved so the account can move forward.


**Billing may identify the issue after discharge, but eligibility resolution should still be coordinated with the team responsible for coverage.**


## The 2027 Changes Make Visibility More Important


For certain adults, the new federal community-engagement requirement generally calls for 80 hours per month of qualifying activities, with multiple exemptions and hardship provisions. States must verify compliance at application and renewal and may conduct additional periodic checks. If compliance cannot be verified, the state must provide notice and time for the individual to respond.


Hospitals should not try to administer the state’s Medicaid program.


That is not Revenue Cycle’s role.


But Revenue Cycle does need to recognize that eligibility may become more dynamic for some patients.


CMS itself has emphasized automation, data integration, and real-time verification as states prepare for these changes.


Hospitals should be asking a similar operational question:


**Will our systems and teams know quickly when Medicaid eligibility changes?**


## What I Would Validate Before 2027


I would want Revenue Cycle leaders to confirm that they have:


- a clear owner for Medicaid eligibility when coverage is not active,
- automated or scheduled 30-day eligibility checks for long-stay patients,
- a work queue triggered by any change, lapse, or update,
- the next known redetermination date captured when available,
- proactive review 30 days before that date when capacity allows, or at least 15 days before,
- next-business-day follow-up when an in-house patient’s eligibility changes,
- a three-attempt outreach process,
- an **Eligibility Unresolved** status with a real escalation pathway,
- and a defined handoff between Billing and the front-end eligibility team for discharged, unbilled accounts.


Not all of those are federal requirements.


They are operational controls.


And that distinction matters.


**CMS establishes the eligibility requirements. Revenue Cycle has to design a process that prevents the organization from discovering a coverage problem too late.**


## Eligibility Needs to Become a Continuing Revenue Cycle Control


For years, eligibility has often been treated as an early Patient Access task:


Verify coverage.


Document it.


Move forward.


For long-stay patients in particular, that is not enough.


Revenue Cycle needs visibility into coverage changes after admission.


It needs awareness of approaching redeterminations.


It needs work queues that react when something changes.


And it needs clear ownership while the patient and family are still accessible.


Because the biggest Medicaid eligibility risk may not be that coverage changes.


**It may be that no one knows it changed until it is too late to do something about it.**
